title: Roulette Variants in Canada: European vs American Wheels
excerpt: Not every roulette wheel is priced the same. Here is how European, American and French variants differ, and which one Canadian players should be choosing.
author: David Andersen
bodyHtml:
Roulette looks like one game. Open the table lobby at almost any Canadian online casino and you will find a dozen versions of it, and the differences between them are worth far more money than most players realise. Choosing between roulette variants is the single easiest decision in the casino, because online roulette in Canada offers wheels whose house edges differ by a factor of nearly four — for a game that plays identically from the player's seat. This guide explains what actually separates the wheels, what the extra zero costs you, and which table to sit at.

The only structural difference that matters

Every roulette wheel pays a straight-up winner at 35 to 1. That number never changes. What changes is how many pockets the ball can land in.

A European wheel has 37 pockets: numbers 1 through 36 plus a single zero. An American wheel has 38: the same numbers plus both a zero and a double zero. The payouts are identical on both. The extra pocket is the entire house edge, and it is the reason the two games are priced so differently.

  • European (single zero): 37 pockets, house edge of 2.70% on effectively every bet on the layout.
  • American (double zero): 38 pockets, house edge of 5.26% on effectively every bet — nearly double.
  • The American basket bet: the five-number wager covering 0, 00, 1, 2 and 3 carries a 7.89% edge, the worst bet on any roulette table.
  • French (single zero plus La Partage or En Prison): 1.35% on even-money bets, the best roulette in the casino.

What the second zero actually costs

Percentages are abstract, so put it in practical terms. House edge is the share of every dollar wagered that the game expects to keep over time. On a European wheel, staking ten dollars a spin means the game expects to keep about 27 cents of that stake. On an American wheel, the same ten dollars expects to lose about 53 cents. Over a session of a few hundred spins, that gap is not a rounding error — it is the difference between a game you can play for an evening and one that erodes your balance roughly twice as fast for exactly the same entertainment.

There is no compensating advantage. American roulette does not pay more, does not offer better side bets, and does not give you a wider range of numbers in any meaningful sense. It is simply a worse-priced version of the same game, and it exists online largely because some players do not check. If you take one thing from this article, take this: unless a table is labelled American or you can see two green pockets, verify before you bet.

How to tell which wheel you are on

Three quick checks. Look at the green pockets on the wheel graphic — one or two. Look at the top of the betting layout, where a single-zero table shows one green box and a double-zero table shows two. And open the game's information or paytable panel, which every licensed provider is required to include; it will state the return to player, and a figure around 97.3% indicates a single-zero wheel while roughly 94.7% indicates a double-zero one. Our overview of online roulette rules and bets walks through the layout in more detail if you are still learning the table.

Why French roulette is the best value on the floor

French roulette uses the same single-zero wheel as the European game, but adds one of two rules that change the maths on even-money bets — red or black, odd or even, high or low.

Under La Partage, when the ball lands in zero, half of your even-money stake is returned instead of the whole bet being lost. Under En Prison, the bet is instead held over for one more spin, and if it wins on that spin you get your original stake back. Both rules cut the effective house edge on even-money wagers from 2.70% to 1.35%, which is competitive with blackjack played at a decent table.

The catch is scope. The reduction applies only to the even-money outside bets. Straight-up numbers, splits, corners and columns on a French table still carry the standard 2.70%. So French roulette is the correct choice specifically for players who bet the outside — and for those players it is the best-priced game in the entire live casino. French tables are less common than European ones in Canadian lobbies, but they are worth seeking out, and they turn up more often in live-dealer sections than in the automated RNG lists.

Live dealer, lightning and the rest of the lobby

Beyond the three classic wheels, Canadian players will find a growing tier of variants built for streaming. These are worth understanding because their marketing rarely mentions their pricing.

Live-dealer roulette

A real wheel, a real croupier and a video feed. The maths is unchanged from the underlying variant — a single-zero live table is a 2.70% game exactly like its digital counterpart. What differs is pace and stake levels. Live tables run slower, typically under a minute per round, which means fewer spins per hour and therefore less total exposure for the same session length. That is quietly one of the better arguments for playing live.

Lightning and multiplier variants

These games add randomly generated multipliers to a handful of straight-up numbers each round, sometimes running into the hundreds. They look like free upside. They are not. The multipliers are funded by cutting the standard straight-up payout — often from 35 to 1 down to around 29 to 1 — and the net result is a house edge meaningfully higher than the plain single-zero game it is built on. If you enjoy the format, that is a legitimate reason to play it. Just do not mistake it for better value.

Auto, mini and multi-wheel tables

Automated roulette spins a physical wheel with no dealer and runs fast, which increases the number of decisions per hour and therefore how quickly the edge grinds. Multi-wheel games apply your bet across several wheels at once, multiplying your total stake accordingly. Mini roulette uses a reduced 13-pocket layout and, despite the friendly name, generally carries a higher edge than a standard European wheel. None of these are scams; all of them reward reading the paytable first.

Betting systems do not fix any of this

Every roulette guide eventually meets the Martingale — double your stake after every loss and recover on the next win. It fails for two boring, unavoidable reasons: table maximums cap how far you can double, and the losing streaks that break the system are far more common than intuition suggests. Progressions such as D'Alembert, Fibonacci and Labouchere reshape the distribution of your results, making many small wins and occasional large losses, but they do not change the house edge by a single basis point. No sequence of bets on a negative-expectation game produces a positive expectation. The only lever a roulette player genuinely controls is which wheel they sit at.

Bankroll pacing and table limits

Because the edge applies to total amount wagered rather than to your deposit, the variable that decides how long your money lasts is stake multiplied by spins per hour. A player betting small on a slow live table can play all evening on a bankroll that a fast auto table would consume in twenty minutes. Set a session budget before you open the game, pick a stake that gives you a few hundred spins within it, and choose a table whose minimum comfortably fits — do not stretch to a high-limit table because the interface looks better.

So what should you play?

The answer is short. If you bet mainly red or black, odds or evens, find a French table with La Partage and play there. If you bet numbers and inside combinations, play a European single-zero wheel. Play the lightning and multiplier variants only when you actively want that format and accept the higher cost. And avoid the American double-zero wheel entirely — there is no situation in which it is the correct choice for a Canadian player who has a single-zero table available.
